title: Thebes, Egypt
wiki_lead:
Thebes (Egyptian Arabic: طيبه, romanized: ṭība), known to the ancient Egyptians as Waset, was an ancient Egyptian city located along the Nile about 800 kilometers (500 mi) south of the Mediterranean. Its ruins lie within the modern Egyptian city of Luxor. Thebes was the main city of the fourth Upper Egyptian nome (Sceptre nome) and was the capital of Egypt for long periods during the Middle Kingdom and New Kingdom eras.
The city was close to Nubia and the Eastern Desert, with its valuable mineral resources and trade routes. It was a religious center and the most venerated city during many periods of ancient Egyptian history.
The site of Thebes includes areas on both the eastern bank of the Nile, where the temples of Karnak and Luxor stand and where the city was situated; and the western bank, where a necropolis of large private and royal cemeteries and funerary complexes can be found. In 1979, the ruins of ancient Thebes were classified by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site.

Toponymy

The Egyptian name for Thebes was wꜣs.t, "City of the wꜣs", the sceptre of the pharaohs, a long staff with an animal's head and a forked base. From the end of the New Kingdom, Thebes was known in Egyptian as njw.t-jmn, the "City of Amun", the chief of the Theban Triad of deities whose other members were Mut and Khonsu. This name of Thebes appears in the Tanakh as the "Nōʼ ʼĀmôn" (נא אמון) in the Book of Nahum and also as "No" (נא) mentioned in the Book of Ezekiel and Jeremiah.
"Thebes" is sometimes claimed to be the Latinised form of Ancient Greek: Θῆβαι, the hellenized form of Demotic Egyptian tꜣ jpt ("the temple"), referring to jpt-swt. Today, the temple is known as Karnak, and is located on the northeast bank of the city. Since Homer refers to the metropolis by this name, and since Demotic script did not appear until a later date, the etymology is doubtful. As early as Homer's Iliad, the Greeks distinguished the Egyptian Thebes as "Thebes of the Hundred Gates" (Θῆβαι ἑκατόμπυλοι, Thēbai hekatómpyloi) or "Hundred-Gated Thebes", as opposed to the "Thebes of the Seven Gates" (Θῆβαι ἑπτάπυλοι, Thēbai heptápyloi) in Boeotia, Greece.
In the interpretatio graeca, Amun was rendered as Zeus Ammon. The name was therefore translated into Greek as Diospolis, "City of Zeus". To distinguish it from the numerous other cities by this name, it was known as the "Great Diospolis" (Διόσπολις Μεγάλη, Diospolis Megálē; Latin: Diospolis Magna). The Greek names came into wider use after the conquest of Egypt by Alexander the Great, when the country came to be ruled by the Macedonian Ptolemaic dynasty.


Characteristics


Geography
Thebes was located along the banks of the Nile River in the middle part of Upper Egypt about 800 km south of the Delta. It was built largely on the alluvial plains of the Nile Valley, which follows a great bend of the Nile. Approximately 4,000 years ago, a significant change in the geography of the Nile River occurred in the Theban region, involving an expansion of the floodplain that increased the availability of arable land. This environmental transformation likely contributed to the agricultural productivity that supported the prosperity and stability of ancient Egyptian civilization during the Second Intermediate Period and New Kingdom onward. As a natural consequence, the city was laid in a northeast–southwest axis parallel to the contemporary river channel. Thebes had an area of 93 km2 (36 sq mi), which included parts of the Theban Hills in the west that culminates at the sacred 420-meter (1,380-foot) al-Qurn. In the east lies the mountainous Eastern Desert with its wadis draining into the valley. Significant among these wadis is Wadi Hammamat near Thebes. It was used as an overland trade route going to the Red Sea coast. Wadi Hammamat was the primary trade route linking Egypt to the Red Sea since Pre-Dynastic times. grok_lead: Ancient Thebes, known in ancient Egyptian as Waset or Niwt, was a prominent city located on the east bank of the Nile River in Upper Egypt, approximately 800 km south of the Mediterranean Sea, and served as the capital of Egypt during much of the Middle Kingdom (c. 2040â1640 BCE) and the entire New Kingdom (c. 1550â1070 BCE). It was the primary religious center for the worship of the god Amun-Ra and the Theban Triad ( Amun, Mut, and Khonsu), featuring monumental temple complexes such as Karnak and Luxor on the east bank, while the west bank housed the expansive Theban Necropolis, including the Valley of the Kings, Valley of the Queens, and numerous royal and noble tombs. The city's remains, spanning both banks of the Nile and covering archaeological areas like the Ramesseum and Deir el-Bahri, exemplify the peak of ancient Egyptian civilization and were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1979 under criteria (i), (iii), and (vi) for their outstanding universal value in architecture, urban planning, and testimony to imperial power. Thebes rose to prominence during the 11th Dynasty when Mentuhotep II (r. c. 2061â2010 BCE) reunified Egypt after the First Intermediate Period, establishing the city as the political and religious capital and initiating major building projects, including his innovative terraced mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri. Under the New Kingdom, particularly during the reigns of pharaohs like Ahmose I, Hatshepsut, and Ramesses II (r. 1279â1213 BCE), Thebes flourished as the empire's heart, with the priesthood of Amun amassing vast wealth and influence through temple estates that controlled land, trade, and labor across Egypt and Nubia. The Karnak Temple complex, dedicated to Amun-Ra, grew into one of the largest religious sites in the world, expanded over centuries with hypostyle halls, obelisks, and pylons, while Luxor Temple served as a key venue for festivals like the Opet, linking the living pharaoh to divine kingship. On the west bank, the hidden tombs in the Valley of the Kings, such as that of Tutankhamun (r. 1332â1323 BCE), preserved royal burials and treasures, reflecting beliefs in the afterlife and the pharaoh's divine status. Beyond its monumental architecture, Thebes was a vibrant economic and cultural hub with a population estimated at around 50,000 during its height (c. 1500â1000 BCE), supporting diverse activities from agriculture and trade in goods like gold, incense, and Nubian ivory to skilled crafts in villages like Deir el-Medina, where tomb builders lived. The city's influence extended through military campaigns and diplomatic ties, underpinning Egypt's empire from the Euphrates to northern Sudan, though it faced disruptions like Akhenaten's religious reforms (c. 1353â1336 BCE) that temporarily shifted focus to Akhetaten. In the Late Period and Ptolemaic era (c. 664â30 BCE), Thebes retained religious importance but declined politically after revolts against Ptolemaic rule in the 3rdâ1st centuries BCE, eventually becoming a provincial center overshadowed by Alexandria, with its temples repurposed or damaged by the Roman period. Today, as modern Luxor, the site continues to yield archaeological insights into daily life, art, and administration, underscoring Thebes' enduring legacy in understanding ancient Egyptian society.
